They found a significant association between rheumatoid arthritis and the organic cation transporter gene SLC22A4 (P = 0.000034).
quotes: We investigated the genetic contribution of the cytokine gene cluster in chromosome 5q31 to susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis in the Japanese population by case-control linkage disequilibrium (LD) mapping using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
Here we report that there is significant association between rheumatoid arthritis and the organic cation transporter gene SLC22A4 (P = 0.000034).

notes.statement: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) found that an intronic SNP in SLC22A4 changed the gene's transcriptional efficiency in vitro. The effect came from an allelic difference in binding affinity for RUNX1, a transcriptional regulator in the hematopoietic system.
quotes: A SNP affects the transcriptional efficiency of SLC22A4 in vitro, owing to an allelic difference in affinity to Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1), a transcriptional regulator in the hematopoietic system.

notes.statement: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) found that a SNP in RUNX1 was also strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.00035). They suggested that RUNX1 regulation of SLC22A4 expression may be an example of an epistatic effect of two genes on the disorder.
quotes: A SNP in RUNX1 is also strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.00035).

Our data indicate that the regulation of SLC22A4 expression by RUNX1 is associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis, which may represent an example of an epistatic effect of two genes on this disorder.

notes.statement: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) showed that SLC22A4 expression was specific to hematological and immunological tissues. SLC22A4 was also highly expressed in the inflamed joints of mice with collagen-induced arthritis.
quotes: We show that expression of SLC22A4 is specific to hematological and immunological tissues and that SLC22A4 is also highly expressed in the inflammatory joints of mice with collagen-induced arthritis.

notes.statement: Schönland et al. (2003) found that HLA-DRB1*04 alleles were associated with excessive loss of telomeres in CD4+ T cells in healthy individuals. The accelerated loss happened during the first two decades of life, and homeostatic T cell proliferation was reduced in adulthood. Granulocytes also showed early telomere loss, which suggested that the hematopoietic stem cell is the primary target. Telomeric repair mechanisms were intact.
quotes: In healthy individuals, HLA-DRB1*04 alleles were associated with excessive loss of telomeres in CD4+ T cells.
Accelerated telomeric erosion occurred during the first two decades of life and was followed by reduced homeostatic T cell proliferation during adulthood.
Premature telomeric loss also affected granulocytes, suggesting that the hematopoietic stem cell is the primary target.

notes.statement: Schönland et al. (2003) proposed that HLA-DRB1*04 alleles, or genes in linkage disequilibrium with them, regulate stem cell replication. They suggested this contributes to the build-up of senescent and autoreactive T cells in rheumatoid arthritis.
quotes: We propose that HLA-DRB1*04 alleles or genes in linkage disequilibrium regulate stem cell replication and contribute to the accumulation of senescent and autoreactive T cells in rheumatoid arthritis.

notes.statement: Vandenbroeck et al. (2003) typed 4 microsatellite markers in a 118-kb interval on chromosome 12q15 containing the IFNG and IL26 genes in 251 RA patients and 198 unrelated healthy controls from Northern Ireland. Marker D12S2510, located 3 kb 3-prime of IL26, was significantly associated with RA in women (corrected P = 0.008) but not in men (P = 0.99).
quotes: Four microsatellite markers, located in a 118-kb interval that contains both the IFNgamma and IL-26 genes on chromosome 12q15, were typed in 251 patients with RA and 198 unrelated healthy controls (all of whom lived in Northern Ireland)

Marker D12S2510, which is located 3 kb 3' from the IL-26 gene, was significantly associated with RA in women (corrected P [P(corr)] = 0.008, 2 degrees of freedom [2 df]) but not in men (P = 0.99, 2 df).

notes.statement: Vandenbroeck et al. (2003) inferred a 3-marker haplotype, IFNGCA*13;D12S2510*8;D12S2511*9, that was significantly underrepresented in women with RA (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.32-0.78; corrected P = 0.03) but not in men with RA. They concluded that common polymorphisms in the IFNG/IL26 gene region may contribute to sex bias in susceptibility to RA.
quotes: A 3-marker haplotype, IFNGCA*13;D12S2510*8;D12S2511*9, was inferred that showed significant underrepresentation in women with RA (odds ratio 0.50, 95% confidence interval 0.32-0.78; P = 0.002, P(corr) = 0.03) but not in men with RA.

common polymorphisms in the IFNgamma/IL-26 gene region may contribute to sex bias in susceptibility to RA, by distorting the propensity of female carriers versus male carriers to contract this disease

notes.statement: Lard et al. (2003) compared the -2849 A/G IL10 promoter polymorphism in 283 RA patients, 413 patients with other rheumatic diseases, and 1,220 healthy controls. The genotype was not associated with the incidence of RA. However, it correlated with disease progression: patients carrying the AG/GG genotype, which is associated with high IL10 production, had a higher rate of joint destruction.
quotes: Allele frequencies of the promoter polymorphism -2849 A/G and carriage rates were compared in 283 RA patients, 413 patients with other rheumatic diseases, and 1,220 healthy controls.
The IL-10 genotype was not associated with the incidence of RA, but instead, correlated with disease progression, as determined by the extent of joint destruction.
A higher rate of joint destruction was observed in patients with the genotype associated with high IL-10 production.

notes.statement: Lard et al. (2003) found that RA patients with the -2849 AG/GG IL10 genotype had higher autoantibody titers at baseline. They concluded that the polymorphism is associated with autoantibody production and the joint damage that follows.
quotes: Instead, patients with the -2849 AG/GG genotype, which is associated with high IL-10 production, had higher autoantibody titers at baseline.
The -2849 IL-10 promoter polymorphism is associated with autoantibody production and subsequent joint damage in RA.

notes.statement: Lard et al. (2003) found that transferring IL10 into fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) with an adenoviral vector inhibited their invasiveness. However, FLS from RA patients who carried the -2849 G allele were no more or less invasive in vitro than FLS from patients who did not.
quotes: Although adenoviral gene transfer of IL-10 to FLS inhibited their invasiveness, no differences were observed in vitro in the FLS from RA patients who were -2849 non-G carriers compared with those who were G carriers.

notes.statement: Suzuki et al. (2003) used a case-control linkage disequilibrium study to show that PADI4 is a susceptibility locus for rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.000008). The locus had previously been identified by linkage studies and includes 4 PADI genes. Suzuki et al. (2003) also identified a PADI4 haplotype associated with susceptibility to RA.
quotes: We used a case-control linkage disequilibrium study to show that PADI type 4 is a susceptibility locus for rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.000008).
Previous linkage studies have shown that a susceptibility locus for rheumatoid arthritis includes four PADI genes but did not establish which PADI gene confers susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis.

notes.statement: Suzuki et al. (2003) found that the RA-susceptibility haplotype of PADI4 affected transcript stability and was associated with levels of antibody to citrullinated peptide in sera from RA patients. They proposed that this haplotype increases production of citrullinated peptides that act as autoantigens, which raises the risk of developing the disease.
quotes: We also identified a haplotype of PADI4 associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis that affected stability of transcripts and was associated with levels of antibody to citrullinated peptide in sera from individuals with rheumatoid arthritis.

Our results imply that the PADI4 haplotype associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis increases production of citrullinated peptides acting as autoantigens, resulting in heightened risk of developing the disease.

notes.statement: Suzuki et al. (2003) found that PADI4 was expressed in hematologic tissues and in synovial tissues from patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
quotes: PADI4 was expressed in hematological and rheumatoid arthritis synovial tissues.

notes.statement: Fisher et al. (2003) did a genome-search meta-analysis of 4 RA genome-wide linkage studies. Besides the HLA locus (P < 0.00002), the strongest evidence for an RA susceptibility locus was on chromosome 16 (P = 0.004). None of the 4 individual genome searches had found this locus to be statistically significant.
quotes: In addition to the HLA locus (P < 0.00002), the strongest evidence for an RA susceptibility locus was found on chromosome 16 (P = 0.004). This locus was not identified as statistically significant in any of the 4 individual RA genome searches.

notes.statement: Fisher et al. (2003) found that 12 genomic regions reached a significant summed rank (P < 0.05), where 6 were expected by chance. Four regions (6p, 16cen, 6q, and 12p) reached P < 0.01, which suggested that a subset of these regions contains RA susceptibility loci.
quotes: In total, 12 regions achieved a significant (P < 0.05) summed rank, compared with the 6 bins expected by random chance. Four of these regions (on chromosomes 6p, 16cen, 6q, and 12p) reached a significance value of P < 0.01, suggesting that a subset of these regions contains RA susceptibility loci.

notes.statement: Nedvetzki et al. (2003) found that synovial fluid cells from RA joints expressed a novel CD44 variant, CD44vRA, containing an extra CAG trinucleotide derived from intronic sequence flanking a variant exon. They detected it in 23 of 30 RA patients.
quotes: Synovial fluid cells from joints of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients express a novel variant of CD44 (designated CD44vRA), encoding an extra trinucleotide (CAG) transcribed from intronic sequences flanking a variant exon.
The CD44vRA mutant was detected in 23 out of 30 RA patients.

notes.statement: Nedvetzki et al. (2003) found that Namalwa cells transfected with CD44vRA and with wildtype CD44v3-v10 bound the same amount of FGF-2 through heparan sulfate chains. However, the CD44vRA cells bound substantially more soluble FGFR-1 and stimulated proliferation of FGFR-1-bearing BaF-32 cells more efficiently. RA synovial cells expressing CD44vRA also bound more soluble FGFR-1 than synovial cells expressing CD44v3-v10 or synovial cells from osteoarthritis patients, and antibodies against the CD44 v3 exon product reduced this binding. The authors suggested that this mechanism may foster the destructive inflammatory cascade in RA.
quotes: Namalwa cells, immobilizing FGF-2 via their cell surface CD44vRA, bound substantially more soluble FGF receptor-1 (FGFR-1) than did Namalwa cells immobilizing the same amount of FGF-2 via their cell surface CD44v3-v10.

isolated primary synovial fluid cells from RA patients expressing CD44vRA bound more soluble FGFR-1 to their cell surface-associated FGF-2 than did corresponding synovial cells expressing CD44v3-v10 or synovial cells from osteoarthritis patients.
A similar mechanism may foster the destructive inflammatory cascade not only in RA, but also in other autoimmune diseases.

notes.statement: Okamoto et al. (2003) used microsatellites in Japanese patients with RA and controls to narrow a second RA-susceptibility region in the telomeric HLA class III region to 70 kb telomeric of the TNF cluster. This region contains 4 expressed genes: IKBL, ATP6G, BAT1, and MICB.
quotes: in a set of Japanese patients with RA and a control group, we previously reported the presence of a second RA-susceptibility gene within the telomeric human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class III region
Using microsatellites, we narrowed the susceptibility region to 70 kb telomeric of the TNF cluster, known to harbor four expressed genes (I kappa BL, ATP6G, BAT1, and MICB).

notes.statement: Using SNPs and insertion/deletion polymorphisms, Okamoto et al. (2003) identified the T allele of SNP 96452 (T/A) as the second RA-susceptibility locus in the HLA region (P = 0.0062). This SNP lies at position -62 in the promoter of the IKBL gene. The -62T/A SNP disrupts a putative binding motif for the transcriptional repressor deltaEF1, so the authors suggested that it may influence IKBL transcription.
quotes: we identify the second RA-susceptibility locus within the HLA region, as the T allele of SNP 96452 (T/A), in the promoter region (position -62) of the I kappa BL gene (P=.0062).
This -62T/A SNP disrupts the putative binding motif for the transcriptional repressor, delta EF1, and hence may influence the transcription of I kappa BL

notes.statement: Okamoto et al. (2003) noted that IKBL is homologous to IKBA, a known inhibitor of NF-kappa-B. They suggested that the MHC may harbor RA genetic determinants that affect both the innate and the adaptive arms of the immune system.
quotes: homologous to I kappa B alpha, the latter being a known inhibitor of NF kappa B, which is central to innate immunity. Therefore, the MHC may harbor RA genetic determinants affecting the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system.

notes.statement: Jawaheer et al. (2002) did a haplotype analysis with 54 markers across the HLA complex in 469 multicase RA families. Besides the associations with HLA-DRB1 alleles, they found at least two more genetic effects within the MHC. One of these lay in a 497-kb interval in the central HLA region that excluded DRB1. It was carried on a segment of the conserved ancestral A1-B8-DRB1*03 (8.1) haplotype.
quotes: The results show that, in addition to associations with the DRB1 alleles, at least two additional genetic effects are present within the major histocompatibility complex.

One of these lies within a 497-kb region in the central portion of the HLA complex, an interval that excludes DRB1. This genetic risk factor is present on a segment of a highly conserved ancestral A1-B8-DRB1*03 (8.1) haplotype.

notes.statement: Jawaheer et al. (2002) suggested that more risk genes might lie in the HLA class I region on a subset of DRB1*0404 haplotypes. They concluded that HLA associations with RA are complex and cannot be fully explained by the DRB1 locus.
quotes: Additional risk genes may also be present in the HLA class I region in a subset of DRB1*0404 haplotypes.
they clearly demonstrate that such associations with RA are complex and cannot be completely explained by the DRB1 locus.

notes.statement: Leadbetter et al. (2002) showed that effective activation of rheumatoid factor (RF)-positive B cells, which express an antigen receptor specific for self-IgG, was mediated by IgG2a-chromatin immune complexes. This activation required synergistic engagement of the antigen receptor and a member of the MyD88-dependent Toll-like receptor family, and inhibitor studies implicated TLR9.
quotes: B cells expressing an antigen receptor specific for self-immunoglobulin-gamma (IgG) make a class of autoantibodies known as rheumatoid factor (RF).

Here we show that effective activation of RF+ B cells is mediated by IgG2a-chromatin immune complexes and requires the synergistic engagement of the antigen receptor and a member of the MyD88-dependent Toll-like receptor (TLR) family. Inhibitor studies implicate TLR9.

notes.statement: Leadbetter et al. (2002) concluded that their data established a critical link between the innate and adaptive immune systems in the development of systemic autoimmune disease and explained why autoantibodies reacting with nucleic acid-protein particles are so common.
quotes: These data establish a critical link between the innate and adaptive immune systems in the development of systemic autoimmune disease and explain the preponderance of autoantibodies reactive with nucleic acid-protein particles.

notes.statement: Barton et al. (2001) investigated linkage in RA affected sib pair (ASP) families to 5 human regions homologous to loci found in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. They detected linkage to 17q22, which is syntenic to a susceptibility locus shared by 2 experimental rat models, in 200 RA ASP families and replicated it in a further 100 RA ASP families. Typing more markers in the area narrowed the linked region to 4 cM.
quotes: Linkage to 17q22 syntenic to a susceptibility locus common to two experimental rat models was detected in 200 RA ASP families and replicated in a further 100 RA ASP families.
Linkage to additional markers mapping to the area has refined the extent of linkage to a 4 cM region.

notes.statement: Barton et al. (2001) showed association with marker D17S807 in the ASP cohort using extensions of the transmission disequilibrium test. In an independent cohort of single-case RA families they found association with two 2-marker haplotypes that include this marker, which narrowed the region likely to contain the causal mutation to about 1 cM.
quotes: Association to one of the markers (D17S807) was demonstrated in this cohort using extensions of the transmission disequilibrium test.

Association to two 2-marker haplotypes including this marker was detected in an independent cohort of single-case RA families, thus narrowing the region harbouring the aetiological mutation to approximately 1 cM.

notes.statement: Barton et al. (2001) described RA as an oligogenic autoimmune disease. They noted that the MHC was estimated to account for only 30 to 40% of the total genetic component of disease susceptibility.
quotes: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an oligogenic autoimmune disease but, to date, linkage and association to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) has been the only consistent finding in genetic studies.
However, MHC is estimated to contribute only 30-40% of the total genetic component to disease susceptibility.

notes.statement: Schaller et al. (2001) found that 64% of patients with RA, but not controls, had increased concentrations of anti-glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (GPI) IgG in serum and synovial fluid. Concentrations of soluble GPI in RA sera and synovial fluids were also elevated, leading to immune complex formation.
quotes: Here we show that 64% of humans with RA, but not controls, had increased concentrations of anti-GPI immunoglobulin G (IgG) in serum and synovial fluid.
the concentrations of soluble GPI in the sera and synovial fluids of RA patients were also elevated, which led to immune complex formation.

notes.statement: Using phage display, Schaller et al. (2001) cloned high-affinity human monoclonal anti-GPI IgGs from an RA patient that were highly somatically mutated, indicating an antigen-driven, affinity-matured response. Immunohistochemistry of RA synovium showed high concentrations of GPI on the synovial lining surface and on arteriolar endothelium, suggesting a mechanism by which anti-GPI antibodies may precipitate joint disease.
quotes: Using phage-display methods, we cloned a panel of specific high-affinity human monoclonal anti-GPI IgGs from a patient with RA. These antibodies were highly somatically mutated, which was indicative of an affinity-matured response that was antigen driven.

Immunohistochemistry of RA synovium showed high concentrations of GPI on the surface of the synovial lining and on the endothelial cell surface of arterioles; this indicated a mechanism by which antibodies to GPI may precipitate joint disease.

notes.statement: Schaller et al. (2001) noted that in K/BxN T cell receptor-transgenic mice, spontaneous inflammatory arthritis resembling human RA is initiated by T cells but sustained almost entirely by antibodies to GPI, and concluded that the immunologic events leading to disease in this model may also occur in human RA.
quotes: In K/BxN T cell receptor-transgenic mice, spontaneous inflammatory arthritis exhibiting many of the features of human rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is initiated by T cells, but is almost entirely sustained by antibodies to the self-antigen glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (GPI).
The results indicate that the immunological events that lead to the development of autoimmune disease in the K/BxN mouse model may also occur in human RA.

notes.statement: Yen et al. (2001) found the KIR2DS2 gene in 83% of 30 patients with rheumatoid vasculitis. This was a significant enrichment compared with 76 normal controls (odds ratio 5.56, P = 0.001) and with 70 RA patients without vasculitis (odds ratio 7.96, P = 0.001). KIR2DS2 was not more frequent in uncomplicated RA than in controls (odds ratio 0.70, P = 0.284), so it did not affect the risk of developing RA itself.
quotes: The odds ratios for patients with RA vasculitis having KIR2DS2 were 5.56 (P = 0.001, RA vasculitis versus control) and 7.96 (P = 0.001, RA vasculitis versus uncomplicated RA; Table).
These data indicated that KIR2DS2 did not affect the risk of an individual to develop RA but was strongly associated with the likelihood of vascular complications.

notes.statement: Yen et al. (2001) found that, compared with controls, RA patients had a lower frequency of HLA-C*04 (odds ratio 0.39) and a higher frequency of HLA-C*05 (odds ratio 2.92). HLA-C*03 was enriched only in patients with rheumatoid vasculitis (odds ratio 3.74, P = 0.003). In logistic regression, HLA-C*03 and KIR2DS2 each conferred an independent risk of vasculitis, and no significant interaction between them was found.
quotes: The decreased frequency of HLA-C*04 among patients with RA yielded an odds ratio of 0.39 (P = 0.024), and the enrichment of HLA-C*05 gave an odds ratio of 2.92 (P = 0.024; Table).

After entering both genes into the model, each demonstrated an independent significant risk associated with vasculitis (odds ratio for HLA-C*03 = 8.6, P < 0.001; odds ratio for KIR2DS2 = 3.69, P = 0.01)

notes.statement: Yen et al. (2001) studied CD4+CD28null T-cell clones from 3 patients with rheumatoid vasculitis and found that 58 to 91% of the clones expressed the stimulatory receptor KIR2DS2, often without the opposing inhibitory receptors KIR2DL2 or KIR2DL3. When CD158b was cross-linked on these clones, it costimulated IFN-gamma production. The authors suggested that KIR2DS2 may have a role in vascular damage by regulating CD4+CD28null T cells.
quotes: Of the activating receptors, expression of KIR2DS2 was prominent and ranged from 58–91% of the clones in the three patients studied.
These data demonstrate that in patients with rheumatoid vasculitis, KIR2DS2 was frequently unopposed by inhibitory receptors of related specificities on CD4+CD28null T cells.
If CD158b is cross-linked in the presence of suboptimal doses of anti-CD3, transcription of IFN-γ is upregulated from 6,628 copies to 63,300 copies.

notes.statement: In a genomewide screen of 257 North American multiplex RA families with 301 affected sib pairs using 379 microsatellite markers, Jawaheer et al. (2001) confirmed linkage of RA to the HLA locus (P < 0.00005; lambda-HLA = 1.79).
quotes: A genome screen for allele sharing was performed, using 379 microsatellite markers.
A nonparametric analysis using SIBPAL confirmed linkage of the HLA locus to RA (P < .00005), with lambdaHLA = 1.79.

notes.statement: Jawaheer et al. (2001) found evidence for linkage (P < 0.005) at non-HLA loci on chromosomes 1 (D1S235), 4 (D4S1647), 12 (D12S373), 16 (D16S403), and 17 (D17S1301), and analysis of X-linked markers suggested linkage to the telomeric marker DXS6807. Stratification into white or seropositive subgroups revealed some additional markers with improved significance.
quotes: However, the analysis also revealed a number of non-HLA loci on chromosomes 1 (D1S235), 4 (D4S1647), 12 (D12S373), 16 (D16S403), and 17 (D17S1301), with evidence for linkage at a significance level of P<.005.
Analysis of X-linked markers using the MLOD method from ASPEX also suggests linkage to the telomeric marker DXS6807.

notes.statement: Jawaheer et al. (2001) noted that several nominally significant regions overlapped loci previously implicated in RA or in other autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (D1S235), inflammatory bowel disease (D4S1647, D5S1462, D16S516), multiple sclerosis (D12S1052), and ankylosing spondylitis (D16S516). They concluded that HLA genes play a major role in RA susceptibility but that several other regions also contribute significantly.
quotes: Several of the regions that showed evidence for nominal significance (P < .05) in our data set had previously been implicated in RA (D16S516 and D17S1301) or in other diseases of an autoimmune nature, including systemic lupus erythematosus (D1S235), inflammatory bowel disease (D4S1647, D5S1462, and D16S516), multiple sclerosis (D12S1052), and ankylosing spondylitis (D16S516).
Therefore, genes in the HLA complex play a major role in RA susceptibility, but several other regions also contribute significantly to overall genetic risk.

notes.statement: Allcock et al. (2001) described haplotypic single-nucleotide polymorphisms in IKBL, a gene in the central MHC that they proposed as a potential regulator of NF-kappaB function.
quotes: Haplotypic single nucleotide polymorphisms in the central MHC gene IKBL, a potential regulator of NF-kappaB function.

notes.statement: Using 18 microsatellite markers spanning the 3.6-Mb HLA region, Ota et al. (2001) confirmed one RA susceptibility gene at HLA-DRB1 and suggested a second susceptibility gene in the HLA class III region, narrowed to a 70-kb interval just telomeric of the TNF gene cluster (TNFA and LTA), between microsatellites TNFa and C1-2-A.
quotes: Statistical studies of associated alleles on each microsatellite locus showed that one pathogenic gene for RA in the HLA region is localized in the DRB1 gene, as expected.

a second susceptibility gene of RA was suggested to be present in the HLA class III region, narrowed to 70 kb, that is just telomeric of the TNF gene cluster (TNFA and LTA) and that is located between the microsatellites TNFa and C1-2-A

notes.statement: Ota et al. (2001) noted that the critical 70-kb segment contained four expressed genes, NFKBIL1, ATP6G, BAT1, and MICB, all candidate RA susceptibility genes, and concluded that their results excluded involvement of TNFA in the development of RA.
quotes: In this critical segment, four expressed genes have been thus far identified, NFKBIL1 (IkappaBL), ATP6G, BAT1, and MICB, all of which are candidate genes for determining susceptibility to RA.
These results exclude the possibility of involvement of the TNFA genes (TNF-alpha) in the development of RA

notes.statement: Zanelli et al. (2001) analyzed 6 microsatellites in the HLA region (D6S1014, D6S273, TNFalpha, MIB, C1-2-5, and C1-3-2) in 132 RA patients and 254 controls and defined 19 microsatellite clusters corresponding to previously described ancestral haplotypes. The MIB*350 allele, part of a cluster often found with DQB1*0201-DRB1*0301, was an RA-predisposing factor independent of DRB1*0301 and of the RA-predisposing haplotypes DQB1*03-DRB1*04 and DQB1*0501-DRB1*01.
quotes: we have looked at the allele distributions of six microsatellites, D6S1014, D6S2673, TNFalpha, MIB, C1-2-5, and C1-3-2 among 132 RA patients and 254 controls
the allele MIB*350 was found to be a RA-predisposing factor, independent of DRB1*0301 and RA-predisposing haplotypes DQB1*03-DRB1*04 and DQB1*0501-DRB1*01

notes.statement: Zanelli et al. (2001) concluded that the telomeric part of the HLA region contains a locus conferring predisposition to RA independently of HLA class II.
quotes: We conclude that the telomeric part of the HLA region contains a locus conferring predisposition to RA independently of HLA class II.

notes.statement: Müller-Ladner et al. (2000) used in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry to study synovium from patients with short-term (less than 1 year) and long-term (more than 2 years) RA. They detected IL-4 STAT mRNA in both groups, with the most intense expression in follicular inflammatory infiltrates. In the synovial lining, both fibroblasts and macrophages expressed IL-4 STAT mRNA.
quotes: IL-4 STAT mRNA could be detected in synovium of patients with short-term and long-term RA. The most intensive expression of IL-4 STAT mRNA could be seen in follicular inflammatory infiltrates.
In the synovial lining, both fibroblasts and macrophages expressed IL-4 STAT mRNA.

notes.statement: Müller-Ladner et al. (2000) found that synoviocytes expressed IL-4 STAT and Jak-1 protein and that stimulation with IL-4 increased this expression, with phosphorylation showing that IL-4 STAT was activated. They concluded that IL-4 STAT-dependent pathways operate in both early and late RA and presumably contribute to inhibitory immune mechanisms in rheumatoid synovium.
quotes: IL-4 STAT and Jak-1 protein was expressed by synoviocytes, and up-regulation could be induced after stimulation with IL-4. Activation of IL-4 STAT was reflected by phosphorylation of IL-4 STAT.
IL-4 STAT-dependent pathways operate in early and late stages of the disease and presumably contribute to inhibitory immune mechanisms in RA synovium.

notes.statement: Cox et al. (1999) studied the IL-1 gene cluster on chromosome 2q13 in RA families using the combined sib-TDT and TDT. Several tightly linked IL-1 cluster markers gave suggestive evidence for linkage in families whose affected sibs did not share two HLA-DRB1 alleles identical by descent. The evidence was significant in patients with severe disease, judged by the presence of bone erosions.
quotes: Several tightly linked IL-1 cluster markers yielded suggestive evidence for linkage in the combined TDT in those families in which affected siblings did not share two HLA-DRB1 alleles identical by descent.
The evidence was significant in those with severe disease, as assessed by the presence of bone erosions.

notes.statement: Cox et al. (1999) found no evidence of linkage to the IL-1 cluster with nonparametric linkage analysis. Parametric analysis gave weak evidence of linkage when marker-trait disequilibrium was included. They concluded that the data gave preliminary evidence for linkage of IL-1 cluster genes to RA and suggested a possible role for the region in severe erosive disease.
quotes: In contrast, there was no evidence of linkage using non-parametric linkage analysis, but parametric analysis revealed weak evidence of linkage when marker-trait disequilibrium was incorporated into the analysis.
The data provide preliminary evidence for linkage of genes of the IL-1 cluster to RA and suggest a possible role for this region in severe erosive disease.

notes.statement: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) studied pristane-induced arthritis (PIA) in rats, a model of RA in which one subcutaneous injection of the non-immunogenic oil pristane into DA rats caused arthritis limited to peripheral joints, with a chronic relapsing course. As in RA, the affected joints were mostly symmetric (85% at day 35).
quotes: Pristane is a non-immunogenic synthetic oil that, after a single subcutaneous injection into DA rats, induces arthritis restricted to peripheral joints with a chronic relapsing disease course.
As in RA, the distribution of affected joints was predominantly symmetric (85% of the affected joints were symmetric at day 35).

notes.statement: In a genome screen of 153 (E3 x DA) F2 rats, Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) found that different phases of the disease were linked to different loci. Loci on chromosomes 4 and 6 (Pia2 and Pia3) affected arthritis onset, and a locus on chromosome 12 (Pia4) was linked to severity and joint erosion. Chronicity was linked to loci on chromosome 4 (Pia5) and chromosome 14 (Pia6).
quotes: Loci on chromosomes 4 and 6 (Pia2 and Pia3) influence arthritis onset, whereas a locus on chromosome 12 (Pia4) is associated with severity and joint erosion. We found that chronicity is associated with a different set of loci, one on chromosome 4 and the other on chromosome 14 (Pia5, Pia6).
All 153 (E3×DA) F2 rats were subjected to a near-complete genome screen using a set of 330 informative microsatellites.

notes.statement: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) found that high serum levels of cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) were linked to the Pia4 region, and that COMP levels correlated with the number of affected paws at day 35. Pia5 lay near the collagen-induced arthritis locus Cia3 and the Lyp/Iddm1 locus, which the authors suggested may indicate a common susceptibility gene for several autoimmune diseases.
quotes: high serum levels of cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) were linked to the same region, during the same period, with an identical inheritance pattern at day 35 (Fig. 2).
One of the loci controlling chronicity, Pia5, is located in the vicinity of the previously described Cia3 locus, which controls collagen-induced arthritis, and the Lyp/Iddm1 locus
This may indicate the presence of a common susceptibility gene for several autoimmune diseases.

notes.statement: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) found that F1 rats from the DA x E3 cross developed chronic PIA, but onset was later and disease less severe than in the DA parents. Females were more susceptible than males, and the Pia2 linkage on chromosome 4 became significant only when females were analyzed alone.
quotes: F1 rats developed chronic PIA, indicating dominant genes, but with delayed onset (P<0.0001) and reduced severity ( P<0.0001) compared with the DA parental rats
Consistent with earlier reports, females were more susceptible than males.
this linkage became significant (Pia2) when only females were analysed, despite the decrease in power by the reduced number of rats.

notes.statement: Cornélis et al. (1998) performed a genome scan in 114 European Caucasian RA sib pairs from 97 nuclear families. Linkage was significant only for HLA (P < 2.5 x 10(-5)) and nominal (P < 0.05) for 19 markers in 14 other regions, 4 of which potentially overlapped IDDM loci (IDDM6, IDDM9, IDDM13, and DXS998).
quotes: A genome scan was performed with 114 European Caucasian RA sib pairs from 97 nuclear families. Linkage was significant only for HLA (P < 2.5.10(-5)) and nominal for 19 markers in 14 other regions (P < 0.05).
Four of the loci implicated in IDDM potentially overlap with these regions: the putative IDDM6, IDDM9, IDDM13, and DXS998 loci.

notes.statement: Cornélis et al. (1998) studied candidate regions at 18q22-q23 (D18S68-D18S61-D18S469) and 3q13 (D3S1267) in 194 additional RA sib pairs from 164 nuclear families; support for linkage was extended only for chromosome 3 (P = 0.002), and analysis of all 261 families gave P = 0.001 and suggested an interaction between this putative RA locus and HLA. The authors estimated the locus could account for 16% of the genetic component of RA and suggested CD80 and CD86 as candidate genes.
quotes: were studied in 194 additional RA sib pairs from 164 nuclear families. Support for linkage to chromosome 3 only was extended significantly (P = 0.002).

The analysis of all 261 families provided a linkage evidence of P = 0. 001 and suggested an interaction between this putative RA locus and HLA. This locus could account for 16% of the genetic component of RA.
Candidate genes include those coding for CD80 and CD86, molecules involved in antigen-specific T cell recognition.

notes.statement: Cornélis et al. (1998) noted that a genetic component of RA has been suggested by familial aggregation (lambda-s = 5), twin studies, and segregation analysis, with HLA estimated to account for one-third of this component.
quotes: Its genetic component has been suggested by familial aggregation (lambdas = 5), twin studies, and segregation analysis. HLA, which is the only susceptibility locus known, has been estimated to account for one-third of this component.

notes.statement: Nanki et al. (1996) used a PCR-ELISA method to study TCRBJ gene usage in the TCRBV5, 13, and 17 families. They studied peripheral T cells from 12 monozygotic twin pairs, 6 of them discordant for RA. BJ repertoires were more similar between monozygotic twins than between unrelated individuals, and the inflammation of RA did not cause specific changes in the genetically determined BJ pattern.
quotes: the BJ gene repertoires of monozygotic twins are more similar than those of unrelated individuals; and (d) the inflammation of RA does not induce specific changes in the genetically determined pattern of BJ expression

These results indicate that the frequency of expression particular TCRBV-TCRBJ recombinants in human lymphocytes is controlled genetically, and is maintained despite the presence of a chronic inflammatory disease.

notes.statement: Nanki et al. (1996) found that TCR transcripts from each TCRBV family showed a distinctive BJ gene profile. This profile was seen more clearly in CD4+ than in CD8+ lymphocytes.
quotes: TCR transcripts from each TCRBV family display a distinctive BJ gene profile, which is displayed better by CD4+ than CD8+ lymphocytes

notes.statement: Hasstedt et al. (1994) used likelihood analysis of 28 pedigrees ascertained through RA-affected first-degree relative pairs, assuming tight linkage to HLA, and found support for an HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus with an allele frequency of 2.16% and lifetime penetrance of 41% in male and 48% in female homozygotes. Inheritance was recessive in males and nearly recessive in females.
quotes: The analysis supported the existence of an HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus, estimated the susceptibility allele frequency as 2.16%, and estimated the lifetime penetrance as 41% in male homozygotes and as 48% in female homozygotes. Inheritance was recessive in males and was nearly recessive in females.

notes.statement: Hasstedt et al. (1994) found that 78% of the variance within genotypes was attributable to genetic or environmental effects shared by sibs. The inferred HLA-linked locus accounted for about one-half of familial RA but only about one-fifth of RA in the population, and the authors suggested that a large portion of RA cases may occur sporadically.
quotes: the analysis attributed 78% of the variance within genotypes to genetic or environmental effects shared by siblings.

The inferred HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus accounts for approximately one-half of familial RA, although it accounts for only approximately one-fifth of the RA in the population. Although other genes may account for the remaining familial RA, a large portion of RA cases may occur sporadically.

notes.statement: Lynn et al. (1995) ran segregation analyses on first-degree relatives of consecutive RA probands, who were ascertained without regard to family history (135 simplex and 30 multiplex families). The most parsimonious genetic risk factor was a highly penetrant recessive major gene with a mutant allele frequency of 0.005.
quotes: First-degree relatives from 135 simplex and 30 multiplex families were included in the analyses.
A highly penetrant recessive major gene, with a mutant allele frequency of .005, was identified as the most parsimonious genetic risk factor.

notes.statement: Lynn et al. (1995) found significant heterogeneity in RA risk by proband gender but not by proband age at onset. Both factors were important, but proband gender appeared to be the stronger determinant: relatives of male probands had the greatest cumulative risk. Log-linear modeling showed that proband gender, familiality (multiplex or simplex), and their interaction were enough to define the distribution of risk in families.
quotes: Significant evidence for heterogeneity in risk for RA was observed for proband gender but not for proband age at onset.
proband gender appears to be the more important determinant of risk, with relatives of male probands having the greatest cumulative risk for RA.

log-linear modeling identified proband gender, familiality (multiplex or simplex), and an interaction term between these two variables as being adequate to define the distribution of risk in families.

notes.statement: Lynn et al. (1995) suggested that families with an excess of affected males with young age at onset may be the most informative for identifying the putative recessive gene and its modifiers.
quotes: For future genetic analyses, families with an excess of affected males having a young age at onset may be the most informative in identifying the putative recessive gene and its modifiers.

notes.statement: Gregersen et al. (1987) proposed the 'shared epitope hypothesis' as a way to understand the molecular genetics of susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis.
quotes: The shared epitope hypothesis. An approach to understanding the molecular genetics of susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis.

notes.statement: Bell et al. (1992) described deficiency of the monocyte ectoenzyme non-specific esterase, occurring in a heredofamilial pattern, in 4 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The deficiency was not associated with HLA status or with rheumatoid factor seropositivity.
quotes: Deficiency of the monocyte ectoenzyme non-specific esterase is described in a heredofamilial pattern in four patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
No association with HLA status or rheumatoid factor seropositivity was found.

notes.statement: Weyand et al. (1992) studied 81 patients with RA and found that combinations of disease-associated HLA-DRB1 alleles correlated strongly with clinical manifestations. Patients with rheumatoid nodules were highly likely to carry two different disease-associated HLA-DRB1 alleles. Homozygosity for HLA-DRB1*0401 was characteristic of patients with major organ involvement.
quotes: Our study demonstrated a high correlation of allelic combinations of disease-associated HLA-DRB1 alleles with the clinical manifestations.

Rheumatoid nodules were highly associated with a heterozygosity for two disease associated HLA-DRB1 alleles. Homozygosity for the HLA-DRB1*0401 allele was a characteristic finding for RA patients with major organ involvement.

notes.statement: Weyand et al. (1992) suggested that the disease-associated sequence motif in HLA-DRB1 plays a role in determining disease severity. They also proposed that the codominant effect of HLA-DRB1 alleles points to a role for HLA-DR molecules in thymic selection in the pathogenesis of RA.
quotes: Our data suggest a role of the disease-associated sequence motif in determining severity of the disease. The finding of a codominant function of HLA-DRB1 alleles suggests that the biological function of HLA-DR molecules in thymic selection might be important in the pathogenesis of RA.

notes.statement: Stastny and Fink (1979) did HLA-D typing in 126 patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. HLA-DW4, which earlier studies had linked to adult rheumatoid arthritis, was significantly less frequent in these children than in normal controls. HLA-DW7 and HLA-DW8 were more frequent than in controls.
quotes: HLA-D typing was performed in 126 patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. HLA-DW4, the antigen found in previous studies to characterize adult rheumatoid arthritis, had a significantly lower frequency in children with arthritis than in normal controls (P less than 0.04).
By contrast, in children the antigens HLA-DW7 (P less than 0.03) and HLA-DW8 (P less than 0.01) were increased compared to controls.

notes.statement: Stastny and Fink (1979) found the antigen TMo, which is related to HLA-DW7 and DW11, in 46% of patients with persistent pauciarticular arthritis of childhood and in only 1% of controls (relative risk 67.7). They concluded that adult rheumatoid arthritis and childhood arthritis differ fundamentally.
quotes: 46% of the patients with persistent pauciarticular arthritis of childhood typed for the antigen TMo, compared to only 1% of normal controls. Thus the relative risk for persistent pauciarticular arthritis in relation to the presence of TMo was 67.7 (P less than 0.0001).
These results provide evidence of fundamental differences between adult rheumatoid arthritis and arthritis of childhood.
